title: What is upcasting and downcasting with B b = new A() vs A a = new B()?
shortTitle: Explain B b = new A() vs A a = new B() with upcasting
keyPoints: Upcasting: assigning a subclass object to a parent reference – Account a = new SavingsAccount() – always safe, implicit
Downcasting: casting a parent reference back to a subclass type – (SavingsAccount) a – requires explicit cast, may throw ClassCastException
The reference type determines which methods you can CALL (compile time)
The object type determines which implementation RUNS (runtime polymorphism)
Use instanceof before downcasting to prevent ClassCastException
Java 16+ pattern matching: if (a instanceof SavingsAccount sa) combines check + cast

s1_definition.oneliner: Upcasting (child to parent reference) is implicit and safe. Downcasting (parent to child reference) requires an explicit cast and risks ClassCastException. The object type decides which method runs.
s1_definition.profdef:
Two directions:

- **Upcasting:** `Account a = new SavingsAccount(...)` – the subclass object is assigned to a parent reference. Always safe, no cast needed. You can only call Account methods through `a`, but overridden methods run the SavingsAccount version.
- **Downcasting:** `SavingsAccount sa = (SavingsAccount) a` – casting the parent reference back to the subclass type. Requires an explicit cast. Throws `ClassCastException` if the actual object is not a SavingsAccount.
s1_definition.analogy: Upcasting: treating a specific savings account passbook as a generic "account" – you can do general account operations but not savings-specific ones. Downcasting: checking that the generic account is actually a savings account, then using savings-specific features. If it is actually a current account, the check fails.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
  Account a = new SavingsAccount(...);

  Compile time (reference type: Account):
    a.getBalance()      → OK (Account has it)
    a.getInterestRate() → ERROR (Account does not have it)

  Runtime (object type: SavingsAccount):
    a.calculateInterest() → SavingsAccount version (overridden)

  Downcast:
    if (a instanceof SavingsAccount sa) → safe
    (SavingsAccount) a → ok if actually SavingsAccount
    (SavingsAccount) currentAccount → ClassCastException!
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Upcasting assigns a subclass object to a parent reference and is always safe and implicit. Downcasting casts a parent reference back to a subclass type and requires an explicit cast that can throw ClassCastException.

The reference type determines which methods you can call at compile time. The object type determines which overridden implementation runs at runtime. This is polymorphism.

Always check with instanceof before downcasting. Since Java 16, pattern matching combines the check and cast in one clean statement.

One sentence to remember: the reference type decides what you can call, the object type decides what runs – upcast is safe, downcast needs instanceof.
